plain_text: A sponge has no neurons, yet slow calcium waves pass from cell to cell and make its whole body squeeze water out together. Sponges already carry many of the proteins later used to build synapses.
milestone: Poriferan Epithelial Bioelectric Mesh (Sponge)
sensory_organ: Ciliated Osculum Mechano/Chemosensory Cells
circuit_motif: Non-neural paracrine glutamate/GABA & epithelial Ca2+ contraction waves
what_evolved: Coordinated whole-body canal contraction without neurons via slow intercellular Ca2+ waves (0.5 mm/s) and proto-post-synaptic scaffold proteins (PSD-95 homologs).
source: Leys et al. (2019) Curr. Biol.; Srivastava et al. (2010) Nature
date_note: Sponge behaviour is measured in living sponges; firm sponge fossils date from about 535 Ma, a debated chemical marker from 635 Ma.

plain_text: Trichoplax, a flat living animal a few millimetres wide, has no neurons. Its cells pass small chemical signals that make it glide, turn and digest food together.
milestone: Placozoan Peptide-Voltage Sheet Coordination
sensory_organ: Glandular peptide-secreting & ciliated margin cells
circuit_motif: Paracrine neuropeptide waves + ciliary Ca2+ gait switching
what_evolved: Coordinates grazing, turning and external digestion across thousands of cells using conserved neuropeptide cascades before a single neuron or synapse existed.
source: Varoqueaux et al. (2018) Curr. Biol. 28:3495; Senatore, Reese & Smith (2017) PNAS
date_note: Placozoans leave no fossils; the date is placed with the first large animals.
date_source: dos Reis et al. (2015) Curr. Biol. 25:2939

plain_text: Box jellyfish have no central brain, only a net of neurons, yet they steer with 24 eyes in four clusters, some with true lenses.
milestone: Cnidarian Diffuse Nerve Net & 24 Lens-Eye Rhopalia
sensory_organ: 4 Rhopalia with 24 Eyes (8 with graded-index lenses) + Statocysts
circuit_motif: Bidirectional ring nerve net + 4 rhopaliar pacemaker ganglia
what_evolved: First true voltage-gated Na+/K+ action potentials and chemical synapses; ring nerve integrates 24 eyes to steer obstacle avoidance without a centralized brain.
source: Nilsson et al. (2005) Nature 435:201; Garm et al. (2007) Curr. Biol.
date_note: Box jellyfish eyes are studied in living species; cnidarians appear as fossils by 560 Ma.
date_source: Liu et al. (2014) Proc. R. Soc. B 281:20141202

plain_text: Worm-like animals gather neurons into a small brain at the head end and a nerve cord down the body, so the senses at the front steer the rest.
milestone: Urbilaterian Centralized Cephalic Ganglion & Ventral Cord
sensory_organ: Paired Pigment-Cup Eyespots + Anterior Chemosensory Auricles
circuit_motif: Bilateral cephalic ganglion + paired longitudinal nerve cords + commissures
what_evolved: Bilateral symmetry concentrates sensors at the anterior head (cephalization), enabling directional klinotaxis/tropotaxis gradient comparison (left vs. right).
source: Arendt, Tosches & Marlow (2016) Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 17:61
date_note: Trails and the fossil Ikaria show animals with a front and back by 555 Ma.

plain_text: The tiny living roundworm C. elegans was the first animal whose every nerve connection was mapped. It shows how few neurons it takes to sense, steer and learn.
milestone: Nematode Small-World Connectome (302 Neurons)
sensory_organ: Amphid & Phasmid Chemosensory Sensilla (32 neurons expressing ~1,200 GPCRs)
circuit_motif: Deterministic small-world connectome + rich-club command interneurons (AVA/AVB)
what_evolved: Demonstrates how 302 graded-potential neurons with gap junctions and ~7,500 synapses generate emergent chemotaxis, thermotaxis, and associative salt-learning via hub interneurons.
source: White et al. (1986) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B; Towlson et al. (2013) J. Neurosci.; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: The wiring is mapped in the living worm; roundworm fossils are much younger, so the date is placed with early worm-like animals.
date_source: White et al. (1986) Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 314:1

plain_title: Big eyes for a top hunter
plain_text: Anomalocaris, a large swimming hunter, saw through compound eyes with more than 16,000 lenses each, wired to large visual centres in its brain.
milestone: Cambrian Apex Compound Eye & Optic Neuropils
sensory_organ: Paired Stalked Compound Eyes (32,000 total ommatidia)
circuit_motif: Retinotopic lamina/medulla/lobula optic lobes + protocerebral target tracker
what_evolved: Stalked compound eyes with >16,000 hexagonal facets per eye triggered the Cambrian predator-prey visual arms race via parallel retinotopic motion detection (elementary motion detectors).
source: Paterson et al. (2011) Nature 480:237; Strausfeld et al. (2016) Curr. Biol.
date_note: Fossil eyes with over 16,000 lenses from the Emu Bay Shale.

plain_title: A stiff rod and a hollow nerve cord
plain_text: Thumb-sized Haikouichthys swam with a flexible rod down its back, a hollow nerve cord above it, paired camera-like eyes and a three-part brain—the body plan of every backboned animal since.
milestone: Cambrian Basal Craniate Dorsal Nerve Cord, Notochord & Camera Eyes (Haikouichthys)
sensory_organ: Paired Camera-Eye Cups + Nasal Sacs + Otic Balance Capsules
circuit_motif: Dorsal hollow neural tube + tripartite forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain + segmented myomere swimming loop + notochord
what_evolved: Establishes the chordate-vertebrate axis: a dorsal hollow nerve cord above a stiffening notochord, paired camera eyes, nasal sacs, ear capsules and gill arches.
source: Shu et al. (2003) Nature 421:526; Shu et al. (1999) Nature 402:42
date_note: Hundreds of soft-bodied Haikouichthys fossils from the 518 Ma Chengjiang shale preserve eyes, nasal sacs, brain, notochord and gill arches.
date_source: Shu et al. (2003) Nature 421:526; Yang et al. (2018) Sci. Adv. 4:eaau8861

plain_text: Lampreys, living relatives of the early jawless fish, already release dopamine when things go better than expected, so actions that pay off get repeated.
milestone: Agnathan Basal Ganglia & Dopamine Reward-Prediction Loop
sensory_organ: Paired camera eyes + pineal photoreceptor + olfactory sac
circuit_motif: Striatum/pallidum action selector + phasic dopamine TD-error signal
what_evolved: Establishes the vertebrate actor-critic circuit: dopamine bursts mark better-than-expected outcomes so synaptic weights (~4.7 bits each) store lifetime trial-and-error lessons.
source: Stephenson-Jones et al. (2011) Nature 479:106; Schultz, Dayan & Montague (1997) Science 275:1593; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: Measured in living lampreys; jawless fish fossils date from about 480 Ma and lamprey fossils from 360 Ma.

plain_text: Early fishes lined their head and flanks with hair-cell canals that feel water currents and unseen motion in the dark, alongside skin pores that detect weak electric fields.
milestone: Silurian Fish Mechanosensory Lateral Line & Electroreceptive Array
representative_system: Thelodus / Early Silurian Jawless & Jawed Fishes
sensory_organ: Cranial & Trunk Lateral-Line Neuromast Canals + Ampullary Electroreceptors
circuit_motif: Somatotopic hindbrain octavolateralis map + cerebellar-like self-motion cancellation filter
what_evolved: Hydrodynamic pressure-gradient canals and weak-field electroreceptors map 3D prey wakes in murky water while an adaptive hindbrain filter subtracts the fish's own fin-beat noise.
source: Modrell et al. (2011) Nat. Commun. 2:496; Bell, Han & Sawtell (2008) Annu. Rev. Neurosci. 31:1
date_note: Silurian dermal headshields preserve grooved lateral-line sensory canals and electroreceptive pore fields by ~440 Ma.
date_source: Janvier (1996) Early Vertebrates; King et al. (2018) Proc. R. Soc. B 285:20172418

plain_text: Jawed fish wrap nerve fibres in myelin, a fatty insulation that lets signals run many times faster without making the fibres thicker.
milestone: Early Vertebrate Myelinated Axons & Tripartite Brain
sensory_organ: Camera Eyes + Mechanosensory Lateral Line + Ampullae of Lorenzini (Electroreception)
circuit_motif: Saltatory myelinated tracts (40–80 m/s) + Optic Tectum + Cerebellar-like lateral line filter
what_evolved: Myelin sheaths (Nodes of Ranvier) boosted axonal conduction speed 50-fold (from 1 m/s to >50 m/s) while cutting capacitive ATP cost per spike by 10x, enabling large predatory vertebrate bodies.
source: Zalc, Goujet & Colman (2008) Curr. Biol. 18:R511; Bullock, Moore & Fields (1984) Science
date_note: Placoderm skulls show nerve openings that imply myelinated nerves.

plain_text: The mantis shrimp's eyes carry about 12 colour channels plus sensors for polarised light. It seems to recognise colours quickly rather than compare them finely.
milestone: Stomatopod 16-Channel Hyperspectral & Polarization Retina
sensory_organ: Tri-artite Compound Eye with 6-Row Midband (16 opsin/filter channels + circular polarization)
circuit_motif: Midband 16-photoreceptor spectral lookup scanner + reniform body
what_evolved: Offloads spectral computation to the eye hardware: instead of comparing 3 cones in a large visual cortex, 16 photoreceptor types + 6 polarization channels classify reef targets directly in the retina.
source: Thoen et al. (2014) Science 343:411; Marshall & Oberwinkler (1999) Nature
date_note: The eye is measured in living mantis shrimp; their relatives date from the Devonian, but when this eye evolved is unknown.

plain_text: Fish that raised their eyes into air could see about 100 times farther than under water. That may have rewarded planning a route instead of only reacting.
milestone: Tetrapod Aerial-Vision Expansion & Trajectory Planning
sensory_organ: Tripled dorsal camera eyes peering above water into air
circuit_motif: Expanded optic tectum + pallial-striatal multi-second path evaluation
what_evolved: Peering into clear air expands sight distance ~100-fold and monitored volume ~1,000,000-fold, rewarding multi-second look-ahead ambush planning over pure aquatic reflexes.
source: MacIver, Schmitz, Mugan, Murphey & Mobley (2017) PNAS 114:E2375
date_note: Tiktaalik (375 Ma) and Acanthostega (365 Ma) show eyes moving to the top of the head.

plain_title: A brain spread into eight arms
plain_text: About two thirds of an octopus's 500 million neurons sit in its arms, which can taste, reach and grasp partly on their own.
milestone: Coleoid Cephalopod Distributed Brachial-Optic Nervous System
sensory_organ: Vertebrate-Like Camera Eyes (20M photoreceptors, polarization) + 10,000 Chemotactile Arm Suckers (10^4 receptors each)
circuit_motif: Hierarchical 3-tier embodied architecture: Central Vertical Lobe (50M neu) + 2 Optic Lobes (150M neu) + 8 Autonomous Arm Cords (300M neu)
what_evolved: Embodied distributed computing: 60% of neurons live in the 8 arms (allowing local infinite-DOF motor control and chemotactile exploration), while the central Vertical Lobe performs mushroom-body-like associative learning.
source: Young (1971) Anatomy of the Nervous System of Octopus vulgaris; Hochner et al. (2006) Biol. Bull.
date_note: The oldest fossil of the octopus and vampire-squid line, with ten arms, is 328 million years old. The tree's 'brain spread into eight arms' sits at 470 Ma, where cephalopods first radiated; free-armed coleoids came later.

plain_text: In a fruit fly, about 2,000 brain cells spread each smell across a sparse code so it can be learned and told apart, while a ring-shaped centre keeps track of heading like a compass.
milestone: Insect Central Complex & Mushroom Body Associative Expander
sensory_organ: Compound Eyes + Antennae (1,300 ORNs expressing 62 Odorant Receptors) + Halteres
circuit_motif: Antennal lobe (50 glomeruli) -> 2,000 Kenyon cell sparse expander (5% sparsity) + Central Complex ring attractor
what_evolved: Classic emergent circuit: 50 olfactory glomeruli project randomly to 2,000 Kenyon cells where APL inhibition enforces 5% sparse firing (C(2000,100) ~ 10^140 combinatorial odor tags) + ring attractor compass.
source: Dorkenwald et al. (2024) Nature 634:124; Seelig & Jayaraman (2015) Nature 521:186
date_note: Winged insects appear by about 320 Ma; insects date from about 400 Ma as fossils and 480 Ma by clock. The mapped brain is the living fruit fly.

plain_text: The first egg-layers on land carried a three-layer sheet of forebrain cortex, the kind of tissue mammals later built up into six layers.
milestone: Basal Amniote / Reptilian Three-Layered Pallium & Dorsal Ventricular Ridge
sensory_organ: Tetrachromatic Diurnal Eyes + Vomeronasal (Jacobson's) Organ + Tympanic Ear
circuit_motif: Three-layered medial/dorsal/lateral cortex (hippocampal/piriform homologs) + Dorsal Ventricular Ridge (DVR)
what_evolved: Transition to land required long-range air vision, tympanic hearing, and vomeronasal chemoreception; the 3-layer medial cortex established hippocampal sharp-wave ripple memory replay.
source: Tosches et al. (2018) Science 360:881; Shein-Idelson et al. (2016) Science 352:590
date_note: The three-layer cortex is studied in living reptiles; the first egg-layers (Hylonomus) date from about 315 Ma.

plain_text: In living bony fish such as the zebrafish, a pair of giant neurons starts a tail-flip escape within about 5 to 10 thousandths of a second, before the rest of the brain has caught up.
milestone: Teleost Fish Brain: Optic Tectum, Mauthner Reflex & Telencephalon
sensory_organ: Tetrachromatic Camera Eyes (UV+RGB cones) + Lateral Line Hydrodynamic Array + Olfactory Rosette (~140 OR genes)
circuit_motif: Dual-speed architecture: 2 ms Mauthner giant-axon C-start escape + Everted Telencephalic associative pallium (hippocampal/amygdalar homologs)
what_evolved: Combines a single-neuron hardware interrupt (the Mauthner cell, which integrates acoustic/visual threat in <2 ms to trigger a contralateral tail flip) with an everted telencephalon capable of spatial cognitive maps and social transitive inference.
source: Korn & Faber (2005) Neuron 47:13; Rodriguez et al. (2002) J. Neurosci.
date_note: Crown bony fish appear by about 250 Ma. The escape neurons themselves are older: lampreys have them too.

plain_text: After the Great Dying, burrowing mammal ancestors such as Thrinaxodon grew snout channels for mobile whiskers and nose ridges that warmed each breath and spread scents.
milestone: Early Triassic Cynodont Trigeminal Whiskers & Nasal Turbinals
sensory_organ: Maxillary Trigeminal Vibrissal Canals + Bony Nasal Scroll Ridges
circuit_motif: Expanded trigeminal brainstem nuclei + olfactory bulb + dorsal pallial somatosensory precursor
what_evolved: Snout nerve canals shift from scaly lip branches to dedicated whisker trunks alongside respiratory nose ridges, letting warm-blooded burrowers map dark tunnels by touch and smell.
source: Benoit, Manger & Rubidge (2016) Sci. Rep. 6:25604; Hillenius (1994) Evolution 48:207
date_note: Micro-CT scans of Early Triassic (~247–251 Ma) Thrinaxodon skulls trace the shortened infraorbital nerve canal of whiskered mammal relatives.
date_source: Benoit, Manger & Rubidge (2016) Sci. Rep. 6:25604; Fernandez et al. (2013) PLOS ONE 8:e64978

plain_title: Balance for running on two legs
plain_text: Early two-legged dinosaurs had large balance organs and brain regions that keep the head and eyes steady while sprinting after prey.
milestone: Early Bipedal Dinosaur Vestibular-Cerebellar Controller
sensory_organ: Elongated semicircular canals + diurnal binocular eyes
circuit_motif: Floccular-vestibular gaze lock + cerebellar bipedal gait loop
what_evolved: Sprinting upright on two hind legs demands continuous pitch-roll balance corrections and head-eye stabilization while tracking moving prey.
source: Bronzati et al. (2021) Curr. Biol.; Witmer & Ridgely (2009) Anat. Rec.
date_note: Skull scans of early dinosaurs such as Herrerasaurus.

plain_text: Tiny warm-blooded Morganucodon hunted insects in the dark with a six-layer cortex and olfactory-hippocampal map that could rehearse paths before stepping into danger.
milestone: Early Mammaliaform Olfactory-Tactile 6-Layer Neocortex & Hippocampal Map (Morganucodon)
sensory_organ: Hypertrophied Nasal Turbinals (~1,000 OR types) + Mystacial Whiskers
circuit_motif: Hypertrophied Olfactory Bulb + Piriform Cortex + Proto-6-Layer Neocortex + Hippocampal Loop
what_evolved: First mammal brain expansion (~50% larger than cynodont ancestors): nocturnal insectivory drove huge smell bulbs (~1,000 odorant receptor genes), whisker touch maps and six-layer cortex-hippocampus simulation.
source: Rowe, Macrini & Luo (2011) Science 332:955; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: High-resolution CT skull endocasts of Late Triassic (~205 Ma) Morganucodon show the first major mammalian jump in smell and touch cortex.

plain_title: Jaw bones become a keen ear
plain_text: Paperclip-sized Hadrocodium freed tiny jaw bones from chewing to form a sensitive three-bone middle ear, opening high-pitched insect sounds and driving a second jump in mammal brain size.
milestone: Detached Three-Bone Mammalian Middle Ear & Second Brain Pulse (Hadrocodium)
sensory_organ: Detached Malleus-Incus-Stapes Middle Ear + Coiled Ultrasonic Cochlea
circuit_motif: Expanded auditory cortex + inferior colliculus + 6-layer neocortical map
what_evolved: Detaching old jaw-hinge bones into middle-ear ossicles unlocked high-frequency insect rustles in the dark and triggered the second major pulse of mammaliaform encephalization.
source: Luo, Crompton & Sun (2001) Science 292:1535; Rowe, Macrini & Luo (2011) Science 332:955
date_note: Micro-CT skull scans of Hadrocodium wui (~195 Ma, Early Jurassic Lower Lufeng Formation).

plain_text: Archaeopteryx's skull shows enlarged vision and balance centres, the brain shape needed to steer in three dimensions.
milestone: Avian Stem Endocast & Powered Flight Cerebellum (Archaeopteryx)
sensory_organ: Avian-Grade Sclerotic-Ring Camera Eyes + Elongated Vestibular Semicircular Canals
circuit_motif: Expanded Optic Tectum + Hyperstriatal Wulst Precursor + Folded Vestibular Cerebellum (3D Flight Stabilization)
what_evolved: High-resolution X-ray micro-CT cranial endocasts reveal volumetric expansion of the optic lobes, vestibular inner-ear semicircular canals, and cerebellum required for high-speed 3D aerial flight control at the theropod-to-bird transition.
source: Alonso et al. (2004) Nature 430:666; Balanoff et al. (2013) Nature 501:93
date_note: Skull scans of Archaeopteryx.

plain_text: One ant has a brain of a few hundred thousand neurons. A leafcutter colony of millions coordinates by scent trails, finding food and farming fungus far beyond what any worker could do.
milestone: Ant Brain & Eusocial Superorganism Stigmergic Network
sensory_organ: Antennae with 60,000 Sensilla & ~400 Odorant Receptor (OR) Gene Types
circuit_motif: Hypertrophied dual-calyx Mushroom Bodies (40% of brain) + Colony Pheromone Trail Stigmergy (8M workers = 2×10^12 colony neurons)
what_evolved: Two-level emergence: (1) inside one ant brain, expanded mushroom bodies encode ~400 cuticular hydrocarbon caste/nestmate odor profiles; (2) across 8M workers, volatile trail pheromones form an external exosomatic synaptic graph.
source: Gronenberg (2008) Myrmecol. News; Hölldobler & Wilson (2010) The Leafcutter Ants
date_note: The oldest ants are in 99 million-year-old amber; clocks put their origin at 140-168 Ma. Leaf-cutting began only about 19 Ma.
date_source: Moreau et al. (2006) Science 312:101; Branstetter et al. (2017) Proc. R. Soc. B 284:20170095

plain_text: Millions of termite workers build mounds whose tunnels use daily warming and cooling to circulate air, keeping the nest steady with no termite in charge.
milestone: Termite Cathedral Mound Superorganism (Queen + King + 2M Workers)
sensory_organ: Antennal Chemoreceptors/Hygroreceptors/Thermoreceptors + Subgenual Vibroacoustic Organs (4×10^6 antennae)
circuit_motif: Diploid Royal Pair (Physogastric Queen + Permanent King) + 2×10^6 Blind Workers/Soldiers + 5-Meter Solar-Heated Homeostatic Mound Lung
what_evolved: Convergent diploid eusocial superorganism: 2 million blind termites (2.5×10^5 neurons each = 5×10^11 colony neurons) interact with soil-pellet pheromones and CO2/thermal airflow gradients to construct a 5-meter cathedral mound that regulates temperature (30±1 °C) and respiratory gas exchange for symbiotic Termitomyces fungus gardens.
source: King, Ocko & Mahadevan (2015) PNAS 112:11589; Korb (2003) Naturwissenschaften
date_note: Termite castes are preserved in 100 million-year-old amber; mound-building fungus farmers such as Macrotermes are much younger.

plain_text: Tyrannosaurus had large smell centres and forward-facing eyes whose views overlapped, letting it judge depth.
milestone: Giant Theropod Hyper-Olfactory & Binocular Predatory Brain
sensory_organ: Hypertrophied Olfactory Chambers + 13-cm Binocular Camera Eyes (55° overlap) + Trigeminal Snout Foramina
circuit_motif: Grapefruit-sized Olfactory Bulbs + Binocular Optic Tectum/Wulst + Elongated Basilar Papilla (low-frequency infrasound)
what_evolved: Largest olfactory bulbs relative to brain size among non-avian theropods (~650–1,000 OR genes) paired with 13-cm human-rivaling binocular camera eyes and snout mechanoreceptors.
source: Caspar et al. (2024) Anat. Rec.; Zelenitsky et al. (2009) Proc. R. Soc. B
date_note: Skull endocasts.

plain_text: Giant plant-eaters such as Triceratops grew bodies of several tonnes around brains that stayed small, a reminder that body size and brain power can part ways.
milestone: Ornithischian Megaherbivore Cranial Endocast (Triceratops)
sensory_organ: Low-Frequency Cochlear Lagena + Olfactory Chambers + Lateral Camera Eyes
circuit_motif: Reptilian-Grade Forebrain + Low-Frequency Acoustic Cochlear Lagena (<300 Hz Herd Calls) + Neck Reflex Arcs
what_evolved: Demonstrates extreme somatic-to-neural decoupling in armored megaherbivores: an 8,000 kg quadrupedal ceratopsian operated with a 72 g brain (EQ ≈ 0.11), investing metabolic budget into a 2-meter bony frill and 3 horns rather than telencephalic expansion.
source: Sakagami & Kawabe (2020) Anat. Rec.; Caspar et al. (2024) Anat. Rec.
date_note: Skull endocasts.

plain_text: Dogs and wolves smell far better than we do: thin scrolls of bone in the snout spread air over a large lining packed with smell sensors.
milestone: Canid Hyper-Olfactory Macrosmatic Carnivore Brain
sensory_organ: Macrosmatic Nasal Scroll Turbinals (3.0×10^8 ORNs, ~850 OR types; parts-per-trillion sensitivity)
circuit_motif: Lamina cribrosa scroll-turbinal olfactory analyzer + 6-layer Carnivore Neocortex (~530M cortical neurons)
what_evolved: Dedicated aerodynamic nasal scroll turbinals separate inspiratory sniffing (5–7 Hz) from expiration, feeding 300 million olfactory receptor neurons across ~811–1,000 OR types for stereo-olfactory gradient tracking.
source: Craven, Paterson & Settles (2010) J. R. Soc. Interface 7:933; Jardim-Messeder et al. (2017)
date_note: The first members of the dog family, such as Hesperocyon, date from about 40 Ma.
date_source: Wang & Tedford (2008) Dogs: Their Fossil Relatives and Evolutionary History

plain_text: Dolphins send out clicks and read the echoes, building a sound picture of prey and seabed with brain areas tuned to very high pitches.
milestone: Cetacean Acoustic-Echolocation Parallaminated Neocortex
sensory_organ: Phonic Lips + Lipid Melon Lens + Mandibular Acoustic Fat Window + Hypertrophied Cochlear Nerve
circuit_motif: Ultra-gyrified 5-layer paralimbic/auditory neocortex + Unihemispheric slow-wave sleep + Acoustic melon-mandible sonar loop
what_evolved: Replaces olfaction with active 120 kHz biosonar clicks: reconstructs 3D internal density images of targets in murky water with microsecond interaural delay resolution while maintaining social signature-whistle names.
source: Ridgway et al. (2019) PLOS ONE; Marino et al. (2007) PLOS Biol. 5:e139
date_note: Cotylocara, 28 million years old, has the skull features of an echolocator; the skill probably began 32-34 Ma with the first toothed whales, where the tree places it.

plain_title: Maps of place in the brain
plain_text: Rats have place cells that fire at particular spots. At a choice point their activity sweeps ahead along possible paths, as if trying out routes before moving.
milestone: Rodent Hippocampal Place/Grid Map & Theta-Sweep Deliberation
sensory_organ: Olfactory Epithelium (1,200 functional OR genes) + Active Whisking Array (20 Hz vibrissal sweeps)
circuit_motif: Entorhinal Grid Cells + Hippocampal CA3/CA1 Place Cells (8 Hz Theta Phase Precession) + Whisker Barrel Cortex
what_evolved: At a maze choice point, the rat pauses (Vicarious Trial and Error) while hippocampal place cells fire in 8 Hz theta sweeps projecting 5–10 steps down left vs. right future paths before committing.
source: O'Keefe & Dostrovsky (1971) Brain Res.; Johnson & Redish (2007) J. Neurosci. 27:12176; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: Place cells are measured in living rats, bats and monkeys, so the map is probably as old as mammals; the date is the rat family's.

plain_text: In a monkey about half the cortex works on vision, through a chain of dozens of areas that feed a frontal cortex holding goals and other monkeys' actions in mind.
milestone: Old World Monkey 6-Layer Visual-Prefrontal Neocortex
sensory_organ: Foveated Trichromatic Eyes (L/M/S cones) + Precision Glabrous Fingertip Mechanoreceptors + Reduced Olfaction (~320 ORs)
circuit_motif: 32-area hierarchical visual cortex (V1->V2->V4->IT + MT/LIP) + Dorsolateral Prefrontal (dlPFC) delay-period working memory + F5 Mirror Neurons
what_evolved: Primate linear neuron scaling (no soma enlargement penalty): >50% of neocortex processes high-acuity foveated trichromatic vision across Dorsal ('where/how' action) and Ventral ('what' object/face) streams, feeding dlPFC working-memory attractors.
source: Felleman & Van Essen (1991) Cereb. Cortex 1:1; Herculano-Houzel et al. (2007) PNAS; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: The oldest Old World monkey fossil is 25.2 million years old.

plain_text: Crows and ravens pack about as many forebrain neurons as some monkeys into a walnut-sized brain, and they make tools and plan ahead.
milestone: Avian Pallial Hyperdensity: Corvid Nuclear Forebrain (Λ_avian = 2.84×)
representative_system: Corvus moneduloides / Corvus corax (New Caledonian Crow / Raven)
sensory_organ: High-Acuity Foveated Tetrachromatic Eyes (UV+RGB + Cryptochrome 4 magnetoreception) + Binaural Barn-Owl-Grade Cochlea
circuit_motif: Unmyelinated hyperdense nuclear Nidopallium Caudolaterale (NCL, 2.85×10^8 neu/g) with orthogonal canonical microcolumns
what_evolved: Solves the flight-mass constraint: by eliminating heavy cortical lamination and local myelin, corvids pack 2.17 billion neurons (more than a monkey's cerebral cortex!) into an 8-gram brain at 1.8×10^-10 W/neuron, enabling multi-step causal tool manufacture.
source: Olkowicz et al. (2016) PNAS 113:7255; Stacho et al. (2020) Science 369:eabc5534
date_note: Neuron counts are measured in living crows and ravens; the date is placed with the crow family's early fossils.

plain_text: Lucy's species walked on two legs with a brain not much bigger than a chimpanzee's, but its brain grew for longer after birth, as ours does.
milestone: Early Bipedal Hominin Endocast (Australopithecus afarensis 'Lucy')
sensory_organ: Foveated Trichromatic Eyes + Bipedal Vestibular Labyrinth + Liberated Dexterous Hand Mechanoreceptors
circuit_motif: 435 cm³ Bipedal Primate Neocortex + Posterior Parietal Visuomotor Reorganization + Protracted Childhood Maturation
what_evolved: Synchrotron CT scans of Australopithecus endocasts (Gunz et al. 2020) prove that obligate bipedalism and prolonged human-like childhood brain plasticity evolved BEFORE major brain volume expansion, freeing the hands for 3.3 Ma Lomekwian stone percussion.
source: Gunz et al. (2020) Sci. Adv. 6:eaaz4729; Harmand et al. (2015) Nature 521:310
date_note: Endocasts of Australopithecus afarensis.

plain_text: Early Homo struck sharp flakes from stone, a skill that ties together eye, hand and force control, and brains grew larger over the following million years.
milestone: Early Homo Parietal-Premotor Stone-Knapping Circuit
sensory_organ: Foveated vision + fingertip force/angle mechanoreceptors
circuit_motif: Expanded Anterior Supramarginal Gyrus + ventral premotor percussive control
what_evolved: Striking razor-sharp stone flakes at <90° platform angles co-evolves with a 50% jump in hominin brain volume (~42B neurons) and hand-eye force prediction.
source: Tobias (1987) J. Hum. Evol.; Stout & Chaminade (2007) Neuropsychologia 45:1091
date_note: The oldest Homo jaw is 2.8 million years old; the oldest Oldowan tools 2.6 million.

plain_text: Homo erectus had a brain about two thirds the size of ours and shaped symmetrical hand-axes, work that means planning many strikes ahead.
milestone: Pleistocene Acheulean Toolmaker Endocast (Homo erectus)
sensory_organ: Foveated Trichromatic Vision + Precision Power/Pinch Grip + Expanded Vocal-Auditory Loop
circuit_motif: 950 cm³ Encephalized Cortex + Asymmetric Broca's Cap (BA 44/45) + Fronto-Parietal Hierarchical Action-Tree Network
what_evolved: Controlled fire and cooking externalized digestion (Fonseca-Azevedo & Herculano-Houzel 2012), funding a doubling of neuron count to 62 billion; Broca's cap enlargement enabled hierarchical multi-step Acheulean biface handaxe knapping and mimetic pedagogy.
source: Fonseca-Azevedo & Herculano-Houzel (2012) PNAS 109:18571; Ponce de León et al. (2021) Science
date_note: Homo erectus skulls from 1.9 Ma onward.
date_source: Ponce de León et al. (2021) Science 372:165

plain_title: The eye compresses what it sees
plain_text: Before signals leave the human eye, layers of retinal cells pick out edges and motion and squeeze the image about a hundredfold onto the optic nerve.
milestone: Human Eye & 5-Layer Retinal Edge Preprocessor (Single Eye)
representative_system: Homo sapiens Vertebrate Retina & Optic Nerve
sensory_organ: 1.20×10^8 Rods (scotopic) + 6.0×10^6 Cones (L 564nm, M 534nm, S 420nm)
circuit_motif: 5-Layer Retinal Convolutional Preprocessor: 126M Photoreceptors -> Horizontal/Bipolar/Amacrine -> 1.2M Retinal Ganglion Cell (RGC) axons (105:1 compression)
what_evolved: Why the eye is a neural computer: 126M rods and cones transduce ~10^9–10^10 bits/s of raw photon arrivals, but the 5 retinal layers perform ~100 GOPS of center-surround Difference-of-Gaussians and motion filtering at just 20 mW to compress the stream into ~20 parallel feature channels totaling 8.75×10^6 bits/s (~10 Mbps) on the optic nerve.
source: Gollisch & Meister (2010) Neuron 65:150; Koch et al. (2006) Curr. Biol. 16:1428
date_note: Measured in living people; the retina's layers are as old as vertebrates.

plain_title: The nose's direct line to memory
plain_text: About 400 kinds of smell sensor in the human nose combine to tell apart a vast number of odours, and smell signals run straight to centres for memory and emotion.
milestone: Human Olfactory Epithelium, Bulb & Limbic Memory Highway
representative_system: Homo sapiens Olfactory Epithelium, Bulb & Limbic Highway
sensory_organ: Olfactory Epithelium (~1.0×10^7 Olfactory Receptor Neurons expressing 400 functional GPCR Odorant Receptor genes)
circuit_motif: 10^7 ORNs (400 GPCR types) -> 10,000:1 convergence onto ~1,800 Glomeruli -> Mitral/Tufted lateral inhibition -> Direct 2-synapse Amygdala/Hippocampus highway
what_evolved: High-dimensional chemical hashing: volatile odorants bind a combinatorial chord of k≈20 out of 400 GPCR receptor types at ~3 bits of intensity each: log2(C(400,20)) + 20×3 ≈ 105 + 60 = 165 bits/sniff. At 1–2 Hz sniffing, nerve bandwidth is ~330 bits/s, bypassing the thalamus to reach the Amygdala (valence) and Hippocampus (episodic memory consolidation) in 250 ms.
source: Buck & Axel (1991) Cell 65:175; Bushdid et al. (2014) Science 343:1370
date_note: Measured in living people; smell receptor genes are far older.

plain_text: About 86 billion neurons running on roughly 20 watts, with a large frontal cortex that can nest ideas inside ideas: the basis of language and long plans.
milestone: Human Brain: Recursive Prefrontal-Language Workspace
sensory_organ: Dual Foveated Eyes (2.52×10^8 rods/cones) + Cochlea (30,000 hair cells) + Somatosensory Skin (2×10^6 receptors) + Nasal Epithelium (10^7 ORNs, 400 ORs)
circuit_motif: 16.3B Neocortical Neurons (Layer 2/3 associative expansion) + Arcuate Fasciculus recursive syntax loop (Broca-Wernicke) + Global Neuronal Workspace + 69B Cerebellar internal-model neurons
what_evolved: Emergent recursive symbolic composition: combines 16.3B cortical pyramidal neurons (~7,000–10,000 synapses each) with 69B cerebellar granule cells to simulate multi-step recursive syntax, Theory of Mind, and multi-hour/year counterfactual planning.
source: Azevedo et al. (2009) J. Comp. Neurol. 513:532; Dehaene & Changeux (2011) Neuron 70:200; Bennett (2023) A Brief History of Intelligence
date_note: The oldest Homo sapiens fossils are 315,000 years old; the modern rounded brain shape was reached between about 100,000 and 35,000 years ago.
date_source: Hublin et al. (2017) Nature 546:289; Neubauer, Hublin & Gunz (2018) Sci. Adv. 4:eaao5961

plain_text: Neanderthals had brains as large as ours, made tools in planned steps and lived in small groups across Ice Age Europe and western Asia.
milestone: Late Pleistocene Sister Hominin Endocast (Homo neanderthalensis)
sensory_organ: Enlarged High-Latitude Scotopic/Photopic Eyes + Derived Human-Like Outer/Middle Ear (2–4 kHz speech bandwidth)
circuit_motif: 1,500 cm³ Elongated Platycephalic Brain + Hypertrophied Occipital Visual Cortex + FOXP2 Articulated Speech Loop
what_evolved: Larger average cranial capacity (1,500 cm³) than modern Homo sapiens, with high-latitude low-light adaptation driving occipital visual cortex expansion, Levallois prepared-core lithic planning, birch-bark tar distillation, and symbolic pigment use.
source: Pearce, Stringer & Dunbar (2013) Proc. R. Soc. B; Kochiyama et al. (2018) Sci. Rep.
date_note: Neanderthal-line fossils from Sima de los Huesos date to 430,000 years ago; Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago.
date_source: Pearce, Stringer & Dunbar (2013) Proc. R. Soc. B 280:20130168

plain_text: In 2012 a neural network trained on graphics chips learned to recognise objects in a million photos, building up edge and texture detectors much like the brain's early visual areas.
milestone: GPU Deep Convolutional Visual Network (AlexNet Era)
representative_system: Deep CNN trained by backpropagation on parallel GPUs
sensory_organ: 224×224 RGB image patches from millions of web photographs
circuit_motif: 5 convolutional layers + ReLU + max-pooling + 3 dense layers trained via SGD
what_evolved: Graphics chips repurposed for matrix multiplication train multi-layer artificial neural networks end-to-end, rediscovering cortex-like edge, texture and object filters.
source: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton (2012) NeurIPS 25:1097; Sevilla et al. (2022)

plain_text: Transformer models let every word weigh every other word. One design scaled to language, computer code and predicting the 3D shapes of proteins.
milestone: Self-Attention Foundation Transformer & Protein Folding
sensory_organ: Text/code token streams + multiple-sequence protein alignments
circuit_motif: Multi-head scaled dot-product self-attention + residual MLP blocks
what_evolved: Dynamic query-key-value attention routes context directly across any token distance, scaling one neural architecture across human language, code and 200M 3D protein structures.
source: Vaswani et al. (2017) NeurIPS; Brown et al. (2020) NeurIPS; Jumper et al. (2021) Nature 596:583; Agüera y Arcas (2025) What Is Intelligence?
date_source: Vaswani et al. (2017) NeurIPS; Jumper et al. (2021) Nature 596:583

plain_title: Billions of brains on one network
plain_text: Today about 8 billion people, most of them online, swap text, pictures and video through fibre and radio links, like one large, loosely joined nervous system.
milestone: Global Human Collective + Exosomatic Internet Nervous System
representative_system: 8.2B Humans Coupled via Fiber-Optic & Wireless Datasphere
sensory_organ: 50 Billion Smartphone/CMOS Cameras, Microphones, Satellites & IoT Sensors + 8.2B Human Sensory Arrays
circuit_motif: 8.2B Human Brains (7.05×10^20 neurons) + Subsea Fiber-Optic Mesh (c/n = 2×10^8 m/s) + 15 ZB Exosomatic Cloud Archive
what_evolved: Planetary superorganism ratchet: couples 8.2 billion biological brains via light-speed fiber optics (2.0×10^8 m/s vs. 80 m/s myelinated axons — a 2.5 million-fold speed-up) and externalizes memory into 1.2×10^23 bits of non-volatile silicon storage.
source: Hilbert & López (2011) Science 332:60; Coupé et al. (2019) Sci. Adv. 5:eaaw2594
date_note: Measured today.

plain_text: The largest AI systems today run on about 100,000 chips and can spend extra computing time working through a problem step by step before they answer.
milestone: Frontier Test-Time Reasoning AI Cluster & Governed RSI Loop
representative_system: 100k-GPU Frontier Reasoning Cluster (B200 / TPUv6e + Governed RSI)
sensory_organ: Multimodal Tokenizers (Text, Vision Patches, Audio Spectrograms, Scientific CSV/LaTeX Ledgers)
circuit_motif: Deep Transformer Attention + Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) + Test-Time Monte Carlo / Chain-of-Thought Search + 5-Gate Governed RSI Verifier
what_evolved: Single coherent silicon cluster executing 3.0×10^20 tensor Ops/s (~2,000× a single human brain's synaptic rate) at 120 MW, using dynamic KV-cache working memory (10 PB HBM3e) and test-time deliberation loops to self-audit scientific hypotheses.
source: Epoch AI (2025); DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025); Levy & Calvert (2021) Entropy; Agüera y Arcas (2025) What Is Intelligence?
date_note: Measured today.
